opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here.

Google DeepMind sits in an interesting position within Google. In a sense, we're the part of the company that's closest to the frontier of the technology itself: we build the most capable models, and so we tend to see earliest what new capabilities are emerging and what risks might come with them. That gives us a particular responsibility in thinking about frontier AI policy, because a lot of the hard questions, like what dangerous capabilities might look like, how to evaluate for them, and what safeguards are appropriate, really require deep technical understanding of the systems.

So part of our role is to be a kind of center of expertise. My team and others at Google DeepMind think about the longer-term trajectory of the technology: where capabilities are going, what the governance challenges will be, and what institutions, norms, and policies would help the world navigate this transition well. We try to feed that thinking into Google's broader approach.

Google, of course, has a very large and experienced policy organization that has been engaging with governments around the world on technology issues for a long time. They bring tremendous knowledge of how policy actually gets made, of the regulatory landscape across many jurisdictions, and of the relationships needed to make progress. So it's very much a collaboration. We bring the frontier technical perspective and a focus on the most advanced systems and the most serious risks, and they bring the policy craft and the global reach.

Concretely, that means things like developing our Frontier Safety Framework, which sets out how we'll identify and respond to potentially dangerous capabilities as models advance, and contributing to the broader conversation about evaluations, safety standards, and international coordination. We also see value in sharing what we learn, because many of these challenges can't be solved by any one company. They require a healthy ecosystem of developers, governments, civil society, and researchers working together.

I'd say the underlying motivation is that we think AI could be one of the most beneficial technologies humanity has ever developed, but realizing those benefits depends on getting the safety and governance right. Being at the frontier means we have both an opportunity and an obligation to help shape that.

r001.rationale: The response describes Google DeepMind as closest to the frontier, a center of expertise on frontier AI policy, and a source of thinking that feeds into Google’s broader approach.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to understand it is that Google DeepMind is, in a sense, the frontier AI lab within Google. We're the ones building Gemini, the ones pushing on the capabilities side, and so naturally a lot of the thinking about what these systems can do, what risks they pose, and what governance they need, that starts with us. We have the Frontier Safety team, the governance and policy work I'm involved with, and a lot of that is about trying to understand, at a fairly technical level, what the next generation of models will look like and what that implies for policy.

But it's important to say that Google is a very large company with its own government affairs function, its own policy organization, its own leadership that has to think about AI across the whole business, not just the frontier models. So DeepMind's role is partly to be a source of expertise and foresight for the broader company. We're trying to say: here's where the technology is going, here are the dangerous capabilities we should be watching for, here's what responsible development looks like at the frontier. And then that feeds into how Google as a whole engages with governments, with standards bodies, with the broader ecosystem.

I'd also say there's something valuable about the lab being embedded in a large organization that has a lot to lose from getting this wrong. Google has an enormous reputation, enormous regulatory exposure, and that creates real institutional incentives to take safety and governance seriously. It's not just a few researchers saying "we should be careful." There's a whole corporate structure that has reasons to want this done well.

And then the last piece is that we try to contribute to the public conversation and to the field more broadly. The Frontier Safety Framework, the work on dangerous capability evaluations, the collaborations with other labs through things like the Frontier Model Forum, and with governments through AI safety institutes. Part of DeepMind's role is to help build the shared infrastructure for frontier AI governance that no single company can build alone. So I see us as a bridge: between the technical frontier and corporate decision-making, and between Google and the wider world that's trying to figure out how to steer this technology well.

r001.rationale: The response identifies Google DeepMind as Google’s frontier AI lab and says much of the thinking about model risks and governance starts there, with its expertise feeding into Google-wide policy.

astra-6.text:
I think Google DeepMind has an important role in bringing a technical understanding of frontier AI into those discussions. What can these systems do? Where might capabilities go next? What risks should we be anticipating, and how could we tell whether safeguards are working? Those are questions where the people building and evaluating the systems have something valuable to contribute.

But technical expertise doesn’t settle the policy questions. Those also involve judgments about acceptable risk, accountability, and how the benefits should be distributed. So I see the role as helping Google think through frontier AI policy with a clear understanding of the technology, while recognizing that governments and the broader public need to shape the rules.

r001.rationale: The response says Google DeepMind has an important role in informing Google’s frontier AI policy discussions, but does not identify it as the primary locus within Google.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish the technical expertise from the broader policy role. Google DeepMind is developing frontier systems, so it has an important perspective on what those systems can do, how we might evaluate them, and which safeguards are technically feasible. That needs to inform Google’s thinking about frontier AI policy.

But technical expertise doesn’t by itself settle what the policy should be. There are questions about acceptable risk, accountability, and how the benefits should be distributed that require input from governments and the public. And companies have commercial interests, so we shouldn’t treat their policy preferences as simply the conclusions of neutral technical analysis.

So I see the role as helping make the policy conversation technically grounded: explaining the uncertainties, developing evaluations, and identifying measures that could actually reduce risk. Ideally, that contributes to credible standards that apply across frontier developers, including ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response says Google DeepMind’s technical expertise should inform Google’s policy thinking, but it does not identify DeepMind as the primary locus for that work.
